question: What were the main goals of the TBC life prediction modeling effort?
answer: The main goals were to develop and verify life prediction methodologies for thermal barrier coatings (TBCs) to enable their use in the 'prime-reliant' mode on aircraft gas turbine engine components.

question: How was the TBC life prediction modeling work structured?
answer: The TBC life prediction modeling work was divided into two phases: Phase I focused on failure analysis and developing preliminary models, while Phase II aimed to produce design-capable models. The work involved contracts with Pratt & Whitney, GE, and Garrett, as well as a grant with Cleveland State University for finite-element modeling of TBC stresses.

question: What were some of the key accomplishments of the TBC work in FY 1986?
answer: Key accomplishments included the development and initial verification of a preliminary life model by Pratt & Whitney, determination of coating mechanical and thermal properties, elucidation of failure mechanisms, finite element modeling of stresses, evaluation of NDE methods, and an engine test conducted by Garrett.

question: What was the goal of the airfoil deposition modeling work?
answer: The goal of the airfoil deposition modeling work was to develop and verify a model to predict the quantity and location of corrodant deposition on turbine airfoils.

question: What were the key accomplishments of the airfoil deposition modeling work?
answer: The key accomplishments included verification of the chemically frozen boundary layer (CFBL) theory and encouraging results with the recently developed local thermochemical equilibrium (LTCE) theory, which agreed within 7% in predicting deposition rates.

question: What was the purpose of the rig/engine correlation work?
answer: The rig/engine correlation work aimed to provide a unique and relatively inexpensive laboratory to aid in the development of environment attack life prediction tools for hot section materials, by verifying advances made in life prediction at pressure levels encountered in gas turbine engines.

question: What were the main elements of the TBC life prediction modeling strategy?
answer: The TBC life prediction modeling strategy involved studying failure mechanisms, mechanical behavior, and model verification, with the goal of developing a comprehensive, design-capable life prediction model for using TBCs in the 'prime-reliant' mode.

question: What was the focus of the in-house rig/engine correlation work?
answer: The in-house rig/engine correlation work was focused on the development of a high-pressure burner rig to complement the contract efforts, in order to study failure mechanisms, model verification, and provide data for the life prediction model development.

question: What was the status of the TBC life prediction modeling work at the end of FY 1986?
answer: By the end of FY 1986, a preliminary life model had been developed under one of the contracts (Pratt & Whitney), and coating mechanical/thermal properties, failure mechanisms, and stresses had been characterized. NDE methods had also been evaluated, and an engine test had been conducted by Garrett.

question: How was the TBC life prediction modeling work expected to enable the use of TBCs in the 'prime-reliant' mode?
answer: The TBC life prediction modeling work, combined with advances in coatings technology, was expected to provide the necessary design capability to allow the use of TBCs in the 'prime-reliant' mode on aircraft gas turbine engine components, where a failed TBC would lead directly to a failed component.
